about: Why an answer engine did not cite your site, as six causes, and what to do about each. The codes are ordered the way a fix has to happen: a page that cannot be fetched cannot be indexed, and a page that is not indexed cannot be chosen. This file is the canonical text. Tools render it with a pointer back here and the date it was last verified.
limits: These are causes for API models with native web search, measured on a fixed question set. They are not rankings, traffic estimates, or statements about the consumer apps. Fixing a cause raises the odds of a citation. It does not guarantee one.

D1.title: The engine's crawler cannot read your site
D1.oneLiner: An answer engine cannot cite a page its own bots cannot fetch. Fix access before you touch content.
D1.detail: Check three layers in order. robots.txt: is the engine's retrieval or user-fetch bot disallowed. The firewall or bot manager: does it answer the bot's user-agent differently from a browser. Rendering: is the content in the raw HTML, or only there after JavaScript runs. The bots that matter for live answers are OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User, PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User, and bingbot for anything that reads Bing's index. A training-bot block is a separate, deliberate choice and does not cause this. A difference found with a simulated user-agent is a lead: confirm it in your server logs before you change a firewall rule. Do not unblock a bot that someone blocked on purpose without asking them.
D1.effort: minutes for robots.txt; an afternoon if a firewall console is involved; days if content has to move to server rendering
D1.whereItGetsHard: The firewall is often owned by someone else, and a scan from one address with a borrowed user-agent cannot see what the verified crawler receives. Server logs settle it.
D1.check: An active probe requests the site as each bot and as a browser, reads robots.txt for each bot token, and counts the words in the raw HTML.

D2.title: The engine searches an index your site is not in
D2.oneLiner: Each engine searches a different index. Being in Google's says nothing about Bing's or Brave's.
D2.detail: Find which index the engine draws on, then check that index. ChatGPT search sends its queries to partner search providers, and OpenAI's help article links Microsoft's privacy statement, so Bing is the index you can check and act on. Copilot reads Bing directly. Verify your site in Bing Webmaster Tools, submit the sitemap, and send changed URLs through IndexNow. IndexNow notifies Bing; it does not put anything into ChatGPT by itself. Gemini grounds on Google: use URL Inspection in Search Console and request indexing for the pages that answer your questions. Anthropic's subprocessor list names Brave Search as the vendor for Claude's web search. Brave has no webmaster console. Its Submit URL page asks Brave to fetch a page again, so submit the pages that answer your questions and make sure your site is linked from pages Brave already holds. Perplexity has no public index check. Read Bing and Google as a proxy for it, and say that it is a proxy.
D2.effort: minutes per site once the webmaster accounts exist; an afternoon to verify a set of sites the first time
D2.whereItGetsHard: Account access. Webmaster verification is a human step, and a new site can take weeks to appear after you submit it. A request is not a guarantee: thin or duplicate pages are crawled and left out.
D2.check: One query per index: a site-restricted search on Brave, GetUrlInfo on the Bing Webmaster API, URL Inspection on Search Console. A check that cannot run is reported as unknown, never as not indexed.

stepsByIndex.bing: Verify your site in Bing Webmaster Tools, submit the sitemap, and send changed URLs through IndexNow.
stepsByIndex.google: Inspect the URL in Search Console and request indexing for the pages that answer your questions.
stepsByIndex.brave: Brave has no webmaster console. Submit your key pages at search.brave.com/submit-url, get your site linked from pages Brave already holds, and check again in a week or two.

effortByIndex.brave: minutes to submit; then days to weeks of waiting

D3.cause: Indexed, but no page answers the question
D3.title: Nothing on your site answers this question
D3.oneLiner: Your site is in the index and no page on it answers this question. There is nothing to cite.
D3.detail: Look for your closest existing page first. If one covers the topic, add a heading that restates the question and a passage of 134 to 167 words that answers it, with the answer in the first 40 to 60 words. Write a new page only when no page covers the intent, and keep it short and specific to the one question. Use the passages the engine quoted from other sites as your brief. They show the shape of the answer it wanted. State only facts you can back with a source and a date. Any structured data has to repeat text a visitor can see on the page.
D3.whereItGetsHard: Having something true and specific to say. A page is usually missing because nobody has the numbers yet, and an answer without them reads like every other page that was not cited.
D3.check: A search restricted to your domain, using the question's terms, returns no page that matches.

D4.title: Your page was there and another source was quoted
D4.oneLiner: The engine found your page, or could have, and quoted someone else. The gap is in the page.
D4.detail: Put your page next to the passages that were cited instead of it. Check in this order. Does your first paragraph answer the question within 60 words. Does it carry a specific number with a source and a date. Is the answer one self-contained passage of 134 to 167 words, or is it spread across sections. Is the page dated and recently reviewed. Does your FAQ or other structured data repeat the visible answer, with one FAQ block per URL. Fix the first gap you find and measure again before you fix the next, so you learn which change mattered.
D4.whereItGetsHard: Knowing which gap mattered. Change one thing per page per measurement cycle, and keep a few pages unchanged as a control, because answers drift with no change on your side at all.
D4.check: The engine's own search returned your site and the answer cited others; or the site is fetchable, indexed and has a matching page, and the answer still chose other sources.

D5.title: This question is answered by platforms, not by sites like yours
D5.oneLiner: The answers to this question go to app stores, marketplaces or forums. Your site is not the kind of source it asks for.
D5.detail: Read where the citations went. If most point at platforms, the question is asking for a listing or a crowd opinion, and no page edit will make one site the answer. You have two honest moves. Rewrite the tracked question to one your buyers ask that a site like yours can answer. Or decide the platform is where you compete, and work on your listing there. Change the question through version control so the old trend ends cleanly and the new one starts from zero. Do not keep a question you cannot win because it has history.
D5.whereItGetsHard: Admitting the question was the wrong one. A rewritten question resets its trend, so write the reason next to the change.
D5.check: Half or more of the competing citations for the question point at platform and marketplace domains.

D6.title: One competitor is the engines' standing choice
D6.oneLiner: One competitor is cited for nearly every question you miss, on more than one engine. The engines prefer that source, not only that page.
D6.detail: List the URLs the competitor is cited from and what kind of pages they are: reviews, a directory profile, press, original data. Those are the routes open to you. Real customer reviews on the platforms your buyers use. Accurate listings in the directories your field relies on. Coverage earned by publishing something worth citing. Pages on your partners' sites. Fix your own page first (see D4), because a mention does not help a page that does not answer the question. There are no shortcuts worth taking: no invented ratings or testimonials, no private link networks, no automated engagement.
D6.whereItGetsHard: It is slow and mostly outside your site. Results arrive over months and are hard to attribute, so record which mentions landed and re-measure the same questions.
D6.check: One non-platform domain is cited in most of the cells you miss, across at least two questions and, when more than one model is measured, at least two models.
